JPMorganChase&Co Interview Experience 
 
Ahaan Desai - TY CE 
Eligibility Criteria  
CS/IT only: 8.5+ CGPA 
 
Introduction 
J.P. Morgan Chase recruits both interns and full-time employees through its 
flagship hackathon, Code for Good, typically held during June and July across 
three major cities - Mumbai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad. 
 
I’ll mention the whole process in short: 
1) Online Assessment - end of March 
2) Hirevue Video interview - one week after the OA, beginning of April 
3) Code for Good Hackathon - June & July, as mentioned above 
4) Results - one month after last hackathon, in August 
 
Application and Pre Placement Talk 
In the beginning of March, we were informed about the JPMC Campus Drive. 
The company took the PPT a few days after, where they spoke about what 
their company does, their values etc. They also gave information about the 
internship itself i.e .about location, stipend etc, and also the timeline of the 
entire process.

Online Assessment 
The OA was conducted on hackerrank. The test could be given anytime 
between 28th and 30th March.  
 
Some important information about the test is given below 
●​ This is a programming test of 100 marks having 2 programming questions carrying 50 
marks each. 
●​ There is no negative marking; the students should try to attempt all questions. 
●​ The time allowed for this test is 60 Minutes. The students can revisit the questions any 
number of times. 
●​ Students have to complete the test in a single attempt/sitting within the above timeline. 
●​ The test is proctored. Switching between tabs, copying from others/LLMs, trying to look 
for solutions over the web or any external sources while attempting the test will lead to 
rejection of candidature. 
Note: Video was recorded in the test. 
 
The following questions were asked to me. I solved both questions in 
python. 
Languages allowed: C++, Java, Python 
 
1. Given an array, count the number of elements which occur more than 
once. 
Example: arr = [1,3,3,4,4], should return 2 
Constraint: Size of array  <= 10^5 
 
2. In this question, we were given a number in the form of a string. What we 
had to do was swap adjacent elements if their parity (odd/even) was the 
same and then form the largest number possible using these swaps. We 
could do any number of swaps. 
Example: 
1. 7956801 gives 9758601 
We can swap 9 with 7 which gives 9756801

We can swap 6 with 8 which gives 9758601 
2. 1806579 gives 1860975 
We can swap 6 with 0  
We can swap 9 and 7, then 9 and 5 ​
Constraints: Number of digits <= 10^5 
 
OA Solution & Experience: 
1. For the first question, I used the Counter data structure available in 
python. I also used a variable 'count' to store the count of the duplicates. I 
iterated over all the keys of the Counter and checked if its corresponding 
value is > 1. If yes, increment 'count'. 
Time and space complexity: O(n), where n is the number of digits. 
 
2. It took me a while to get the second question right. First I tried the brute 
force approach, but it did not pass all testcases. In the end, I grouped the 
array into contiguous sequences of elements with the same parity, sorted 
them in reversed order, then joined them back and returned it. 
Why this works: Sorting can be represented as swapping adjacent elements 
until some order is achieved (Bubble sort). So instead of actually swapping 
adjacent just group them and sort using inbuilt sorting, which then reduces 
the time complexity. 
Time and space complexity: O(nlogn) , O(n) resp. 
 
OA Results: 
Around 13 people got selected from the OA.

Video Interview 
The next step of the recruiting process is a video interview on HireVue. In 
this HireVue interview, you will be asked to record video responses to 2 
interview questions. 
 
My questions were something along the lines of: 
1. Talk about an instance where you have worked on a group project. 
Describe your tasks and the outcome. 
2. What steps have you taken to learn about this program? 
 
A question appears on the screen for which, 
1. You are initially given 30 seconds to prepare your response 
2. The recording starts automatically after that 
3. After recording the first response (maximum 3 minutes limit), you click 
done and it gives you an option to retry or submit the recording. You can 
also preview the recording just made. 
4. After your first recording, there is no time limit to choose between retry 
and submit. 
5. But once you click retry and record your response, the next response is 
submitted automatically, and you can't preview it. 
 
Video Interview results: 
4 students were selected from the video interview.

Pre hackathon events: 
1. JPMC sent out the RSVP for the Hackathon, in which you had to fill in 
some information along with development preferences 
(frontend/backend/fullstack). 
2. They conducted online workshops on various topics, as well as an 
office-hours session where they resolved doubts regarding travel, what to 
bring etc. 
 Workshops conducted  
        - Git/Github Workshop 
        - Hackathon survival guide 
        - Prompt Engineering at a hackathon 
3. 4 days before the hackathon they sent out the team mappings and I 
connected with my teammates over linkedin. 
4. They sent out slack and github invites (for the repository where you will 
build your project) on the day of the hackathon itself. 
 
Code for Good Hackathon 
The hackathon was conducted on 7th-8th June at the Goregaon office, from 
5pm to next day 4:30 pm. 
 
I arrived at around 4pm and met with my teammates and VJTI friends. The 
kickoff was at 5/5:30 pm, where they spoke about the hackathon, and laid 
out the flow of events for the Hackathon. In this, the respective NGOs also 
presented their problem statements. Then they made us fill a form for the 
problem statement selection, which was allotted based on first come first 
serve. Luckily, we were allotted our first choice itself.  There were a total of 
27 teams and 3 problem statements, so 9 teams each for each problem 
statement. Alongside all this we also met with our first mentor for the event.

After this, a panel session was held where each team could ask questions to 
the NGO members to clarify the requirements of the project. Make sure to 
participate in this and get all your doubts related to the problem statement 
clear.  
 
We chose the problem statement from the NGO Purnata, which deals in 
rescue and rehabilitation of human trafficking victims. They wanted a 
solution to digitise all their data related to the work they do.  
 
Once the panel session got over, we headed up to where the employees 
work, and set up our laptops. Then we had a brainstorming session with our 
mentor, in which we decided the exact requirements for the project, what is 
to be stored in the database, etc. We drew out tables and descriptions on an 
A2 sheet they had provided us. After this we had dinner, and only started 
proper coding at around 10:30pm. 
 
My team consisted of 4 frontend developers, and 3 backend developers 
(including me). Us backend guys were implementing routes, setting up the 
GitHub repo while the frontend team were designing the entire UI and 
making the initial pages. We used AI to the maximum as they had allowed us 
to. I also implemented an AI feature that my mentor had suggested during 
the initial discussion. At around 3 am we finished most of the backend, 
frontend guys were still making forms and the like. We presented our project 
idea and backend to the second mentor, who had come by then and she 
appreciated the backend that we had made. We took a lot of breaks in 
between, snacks were good and they had fun sessions in between as well.  
 
The biggest challenge for us was integrating the frontend and the backend. 
The frontend team was not very well versed with API integrations so this was 
a challenge. The routes were working on postman but not when it was

fetched in the frontend. At this point we were also very tired so it was 
tougher to get it working. In the end we left it incomplete only and started 
working on the demo and presentation, as these are also important and that 
is what the panel will see while presenting.  
The deadline for PPT submission was at 11 am. After that we presented our 
project and the panel seemed to like it as well. But unfortunately, we did not 
get selected for presenting in front of the NGO members.  
 
After lunch, presentations in front of NGOs, and prize distribution for 
winners, the hackathon was over. It was a great experience, and while we 
weren't able to complete our project, I learnt a lot and had lots of fun.  
 
Results for internship are not dependent on if you win or not at the 
hackathon. Rather it depends on how well you contribute and communicate 
during the hackathon itself. 
 
Results 
The results were announced mid August. Out of the 4 selected, 3 were 
offered an internship, including me. But, at this point I’d already accepted an 
internship offer from Goldman Sachs. 
 
 
Final thoughts 
The JPMC process is quite lengthy (around 5 months). During this time, it’s 
important to continue preparing for DSA and other companies’ recruitment 
processes. You might secure another offer before JPMC concludes. Even if 
your hackathon goes well, don’t pause your preparation. Keep practicing 
consistently until the final JPMC results are out.

Tips for doing well in CFG 
1. Since there are no personal interviews and problem solving/DSA (after the 
OA), the only thing you really need to focus on is development. 
2. JPMC allows you to choose your tech stack preference before the 
hackathon itself - frontend/backend/fullstack. At this point you should be 
well versed with one of these. But if you have not started with anything, I’d 
recommend getting an idea of both frontend and backend, so at least you 
can help out a little bit during the hackathon itself. 
3. If you’ve already started backend, then focus on strengthening your 
fundamentals in building APIs. Be comfortable with an easy to use 
framework such as Express.js, Flask etc. and understand how to design REST 
endpoints. Pick up some databases as well, MongoDB and Postgres/MySQL 
are preferred choices. Keep things simple - no need for implementing 
hardcore authentication, security, deployment. 
4. If you’ve already started frontend, then sharpen your skills in building 
responsive and interactive UIs. Pick a frontend framework like React (highly 
preferred) and practice building components that consume APIs. API 
integration is a must, our team lacked there. It's better if the frontend team 
is aware of API integration as then the backend team won't have to interfere. 
Focus on clean UI/UX because judges value polished solutions. During 
hackathons, frontends are often the face of your project, so the ability to 
quickly prototype and make it visually appealing is crucial.  
5. Fullstack awareness is important, don’t just focus on one side and be 
completely unaware of the other, some knowledge is always helpful. 
5. Having knowledge about Machine Learning, Generative AI and Agentic AI 
is also helpful as it makes your solution stand out from others and many 
hackathon solutions that win involve some part of this.  
6. Connect and start talking with your teammates as soon as the allotment 
list comes out. You can decide the tech stack and roles that everyone will

take. If you don't know the tech stack chosen, you can pick up some part of 
it before the hackathon. 
7. During the hackathon itself, make sure there is proper communication 
between all team members, and voice your opinions and ideas clearly. There 
should be minimal conflict in the team. Regularly track the progress of the 
project as it's easy to lose track. Mentors see all this and the company offers 
you an internship based on these parameters.  
8. Make sure to take breaks as well, there is no need to use the whole time 
for coding. The company also organises fun events/sessions in between to 
keep everyone relaxed, awake and at ease.  
 
OA Tips 
1. Take part in CP contests to sharpen your problem-solving speed. For OA’s 
I'd recommend pure CP based contests like on CodeChef and CodeForces 
(first few questions of contests), as many OA questions are based on pure 
logic and not on any core DSA concept. Some companies tend to ask 
extremely hard OA questions, so I’d recommend trying later questions also, 
and to at least have some knowledge about advanced data structures used 
in competitive programming. For example, the 2nd question of the HILTI OA 
was based on advanced data structures for many candidates, and the BNY 
OA was like a CF contest only (read Siddhesh Pandey’s experience for BNY).   
2. Use a language you are comfortable with (preferably the same language 
used for contests) and have a good grasp on the syntax and inbuilt libraries 
and data structures for a particular language. Examples would include STL 
for C++, collections for python and java etc. You should mainly know how to 
sort, how to use arrays/vectors (depending on your language), HashMaps 
and HashSets. 
3. Read the complexity guide on codeforces, to know what time complexity 
is expected based on constraints on data. This helps in OAs, contests and 
problem solving in general.
